card: Hegel reached Vienna after 6 the previous evening, travelling 42 miles from Prague in 36 hours by express coach with a couple returning from Karlsbad and Archduke Charles's physician. He took a room at the Erzherzog Karl, went to the Italian opera, a Mercadante piece with Rubini, Donzelli, Lablache and Eckerlin, and then found Lilli and Klein at the inn.
X:
Vienna, 21st Sept.

My dearest Marie,

I have reached Vienna safely, after a long, dusty journey of forty-two miles from Prague. We travelled in an express coach with a couple returning from Karlsbad and the Archduke’s physician. The hours were long, but the company kept the time passing.

I took a room at the Erzherzog Karl and spent the evening at the Italian opera. It was a Mercadante piece, with Rubini, Donzelli, Lablache, and Eckerlin singing. I must confess, the music was quite charming, a welcome relief after the road.

Before bed, I found Lilli and Klein at the inn. We had a pleasant chat over wine. I miss you and the boys terribly. Please do not worry about me; I am well. I look forward to our reunion.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: Good morning, my dear! — in Vienna — yes, Vienna; — but unfortunately you are not in Vienna.... So, to get to Vienna, I stayed until Saturday afternoon — up to that point, the report of my last [journey] is in Prague. — Everything in order, we drove out of the gate at 6 in the morning (the express coach tripled). The main coach, mine, is divided into two rooms, which are connected by a kind of window, with 4 persons in each. My 3 companions were a gentleman and his wife, returning from Carlsbad, the third being the personal physician to Archduke Charles for 24 years, who had now retired into an independent position, — so that we were very satisfied with one another on all sides and covered this road of 42 miles in 36 hours, up hill, down dale — day and night on, back and forth. Bohemia — monotonous, fertile farmland, — then through a piece of Moravia, Collin, Czaslau, Iglau, Znaim, — then into proper Austria, — here wine country, fields, hills, forests, one place after another, wide views into these rich regions, a splendid land — at the penultimate station we came near the Danube, — without yet seeing it, — onto a low plain, so for half a day on, — monotonous, one has no view of Vienna here, — after 6 o'clock in Vienna itself, then toll, post, — cab, to look for an inn, received a room in the Erzherzog Karl facing the courtyard, one flight up, — those facing the front are not for us; when I asked about Mr. D. Parthey, it turned out that the young married couple Klein!) were lodging here, but had just gone out; — I then accepted a porter and in travel grime (the trunk is still at the toll house, at 7 o'clock I had arrived at the inn), at ¼8 — to the Italian Opera, for Mde Milder, whom I must mention again later, had so commanded?). — A piece by Mercadante, Mde Fodor does not appear in it — but what male voices! Two tenors, Rubini and Donzelli, what throats, what manner, sweetness, volubility, strength, tone, one must hear it! — a duet of theirs of the highest force. The bassist Lablachen) had no leading role, but even here, how I had to admire his beautiful, powerful, as well as sweet bass voice. Yes, these male voices one must hear, that is tone, purity, strength, complete freedom, etc., etc. They also have a German singer, she is called Eckerlin, who has beautiful, full, strong middle tones, which reminded me of Milder, yet only Mde Milder could match those three male voices and keep them in check. Mde Fodor will play in Othello today. — As long as the money lasts to pay for the Italian Opera and the return journey, — I will stay in Vienna! After the opera and a pas de deux by 2 Parisians — all as good as the Berliners, — if the Berlin women would only stretch out a right angle, up to the obtuse — home, where, to our mutual heartfelt pleasure, I found Lilli and Klein (Parthey's young wife was unwell in her room); that is now very pleasant to me, they are staying here this week and we have already engaged to go around together; they were surprised that I come from the Italian Opera, they have been at the Casperl and German theater every evening for three days and have not yet seen the Italian Opera!! and not yet heard it!! This morning it goes to Belvedere (imperial picture gallery), to the post — to collect letters from you, to the toll house, — to settle passport matters.

card: The previous day Hegel and Cousin went from Cologne to Bonn, visiting Windischmann and then, together, Herr von Schlegel. That morning they saw Cologne Cathedral again, the Wallraff collection and the Dying Mary, and ate oysters with Moselle wine. At midday Hegel travelled alone to Elberfeld, crossing the Wupper again, among students smoking pipes.
X:
My dear Marie,

I am now sitting in Elberfeld and writing to you from the quiet of the evening. Yesterday was full of impressions. In Bonn we visited Windischmann, and we spent some hours with Mr. von Schlegel. The paintings, especially the Dying Mary, have not yet let me go. The oyster with the Mosel wine was a small but pleasant enjoyment.

This morning I crossed the Wupper alone to Elberfeld. The sight of the students smoking their pipes there was a strange mix of youth and melancholy. It is a quiet area, but the thoughts here are not quieter, only differently ordered.

Think of me when you instruct the boys about their duties; discipline is the foundation on which freedom later builds. I send you my regards and kiss you.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel
Y: Now, however, also about our journey; — I wrote to you from Brussels, — in this letter you will find when we departed, — I believe it was Monday, after we had previously in the evening watched the illumination in the city on the occasion of the Queen’s first appearance — the sister of our King!) — So first via Leuven to Liège — a rich country — the next day to Aachen — saw the Cathedral with lights and [we] sat again on Emperor Charles’s throne, then to Cologne — both short day’s journeys — from Liège to Aachen, especially beautiful and rich countryside, — in Liège as in Leuven and Ghent beautiful university buildings; we looked around at these universities, as a future place of rest, if the priests in Berlin finally drive me out of the Copper Ditch entirely; the Curia in Rome would in any case be a more honorable opponent, than the wretchedness of a wretched priestly rabble in Berlin). So arrived in Cologne on Wednesday afternoon, immediately collected your dear letter, — thereby learned that the express mail only reaches Cassel on Friday, i.e. today, — then still in Cologne, — instead of vegetating in this old, ugly city among curiosities on Thursday, made a detour to Bonn, the dear, old friend Windischmann on my part — and then jointly Mr. v. Schlegel“) — first his house by force — and when he had finally come out of it — visited him with all cordiality and cheerfulness — however, the good or rather most stately — and comfortable arrangement of the house — except for the chicken yard and the peacock perch and their painting and arrangement — I reserve for the oral description; only of a woman, whom one might look for there, there is nothing to mention; yet one does not miss her entirely, for if not female, then something feminine is perhaps already found there. — We could indeed have spent several days pleasantly and seriously (though we are generally not inclined to do so) and interestingly in Bonn. That we spent this morning usefully with another visit to the sublime Cathedral, the Wallraf collection, inspection of the dying Marie etc., eating oysters, drinking Mosel wine etc., — must conclude with the addition, that I then alone arrived here at noon with a second crossing of the Wupper in the company of some student tobacco pipes.

card: Hegel visited Schönbrunn again in the afternoon, including the menagerie grounds, where he saw only the elephant and the ostrich because the others had already retired for the night. It was too dark to see the plants. In the evening, with no Fodor, Dardanelli or Lablache performing, he saw part of a Leopoldstadt theatre piece and brought away the playbill.
X: All the rooms in Berlin, Potsdam, and Sanssouci, where I wanted to see something, cost one ducat — or should cost! I will advise my acquaintances who might like to see works of art to take the ducats and thalers that are required for everything and anything — even the grave not only of Frederick the Great but also of his dogs in Sanssouci — and use them to cover the travel expenses to Vienna, and then see here the most magnificent treasures, more in reality than they can currently see in Berlin. — Read some of this to my so dear and worthy friend, Privy Councillor Schulze, — precisely so that he may rightly perceive my gratitude from it for all the love and goodness that has come to me through his benevolent, heartfelt interest, and assure him that, despite all the above, I have given the professors here the opportunity to see that we have no one to envy — on the contrary! — But in order to forcibly return to my report, I briefly report that this afternoon I visited the beautiful Schönbrunn with its views once more, also the menagerie, though only the layout and of the beast population only the royal ones, the elephant and the ostrich, — the rest of the rabble had already gone to sleep. Likewise the plants, and since the flowers do not show themselves with a lantern, I have also spared this for another time — finally — today no Fodor, no Dardanelli, no Lablache, no etc.! The end is bad — everything is bad, namely still a piece of a Leopoldstheater piece, of which I bring the slip. — Tomorrow at the crack of dawn onto the galloping carriage — God guide the driver! This is all that the wishes of my breast are limited to for the time being
Y:
My dear Marie,

Vienna is quiet this evening. Without Fodor, Dardanelli, or Lablache, I felt the absence of their voices painfully. I went to the Leopoldstadt Theatre; it was an ordinary play, but I took the program with me to show you when I return.

In the afternoon, I visited Schönbrunn. The menagerie was already half closed. I only saw the elephant and the ostrich. The other animals had been withdrawn. It was too dark to make out the plants in the greenhouse. One cannot see many things here as they truly are because of the lack of light.

Think of me while I sit in this cold hall. I will soon return to Berlin, where the warmth of our room awaits me. Kiss Karl and Immanuel for me.

Your G. Hegel

card: Hegel travelled on past towns, many sea-going ships and wide green meadows, in good weather, and arrived in The Hague after 8 in the evening. This was the farthest point of his journey, from which he would turn back, but first he planned to see the North Sea the next day.
X: Things are moving quickly, beautiful roads, beautiful cities, ships on the sea in great abundance — wide green meadows, everything charming, prosperous, — good weather — and it keeps going on — and it keeps going on and wider. But this is the farthest point and now it will have to go back. This evening after 8 o'clock I arrived here, but tomorrow the North Sea must still be seen, one cannot resist this temptation.
Y:
My dear Marie,

I am writing to you from The Hague, where I arrived today after 8 o'clock. The journey through Holland was pleasant; the weather was wonderful, the landscape endlessly flat, dotted with ships and green meadows. It is a country that lives by trade and freedom, yet it lacks the depth of the historical spirit that we know in Germany. Here everything is external, visible, clear – like the North Sea, which I intend to visit tomorrow.

Think of me when you think of the sea. Karl and Immanuel may be well; Ludwig too. I will perhaps bring you a small memento from here, if time permits. Until I am back in Berlin, I write rarely. Forgive me the silence.

Your G. W. F. Hegel

card: The previous morning Hegel and his companion had crossed the Scheldt into Antwerp, a city of 60,000 to 70,000 inhabitants, as is Ghent. He visited the cathedral, whose nave has 3 rows of columns on each side and no pews or benches; each visitor takes one of a stack of 100 chairs and carries it from altar to altar.
X:
My dear Marie,

The air in the Netherlands is sharp, but the evening here in The Hague is mild. I have crossed the Scheldt and lingered in Antwerp, a city of some sixty thousand souls, not unlike Ghent. The cathedral there struck me with a peculiar force. There are no fixed pews, only three rows of columns on each side of the nave. Instead, a stack of a hundred chairs stands ready; each visitor must take one and carry it from altar to altar. It is a strange, active piety, where devotion is not passive reception but a physical journey through the sacred space. I find myself thinking how little we understand of the forms of freedom until we see them enacted in the body.

My thoughts turn to the boys and the quiet of our Berlin rooms. I am well, though the journey is tiring. I hope the autumn has settled gently into your day.

Your affectionate
G. Hegel
Y: Yesterday morning we crossed the beautiful, broad, stately Scheldt into the great Antwerp, again with 60–70,000 inhabitants; Ghent has just as many. In these cities one must see the churches! In Antwerp the world-famous Cathedral—in the nave of it, as in the unfinished cathedral in Cologne, 3 rows of columns on each side; how spacious and free one wanders about in it!—The spaces are not blocked up with church pews and benches, there is no bench in it, everything free, but there stands a pile of 100 chairs stacked up, of which each person who comes has one given to them, carries it from one altar to another;—here a small group, there a crowd, always changing, coming and going. The Hague, 9th Oct. Evening.

card: In Coblenz, Hegel had been shown rooms that were bomb-proof and dry, with the explanations given in local dialect, and had to change into his third shirt of the day. It rained without stopping that afternoon, so he slept. He was going to a meal, meant to visit Government Councillor Lange that evening, and planned Bonn next, then Cologne.
X:
My dear Marie,

Coblenz received me well today. They showed me rooms which, as I was assured, were bomb-proof and dry. The explanation was given in a dialect that I could only with difficulty understand, which is why I had to change my shirt for the third time that day with a certain unease. The rain has let up, and I have slept, which could do me good.

This evening I dined with Government Councillor Lange. We spoke about various things, which amused me. Tomorrow I am travelling to Bonn and then to Cologne. I am thinking of you and the children. Please be well.

Your faithful
G. W. F. Hegel
Y: dialect explained the things; they are very nice rooms, bulletproof and dry. — But I am not dry; I must truly put on the third shirt today; you see that I do not lack in movement, also in marching, and that the hardships keep me in good health. Now it is time for dinner, and although satiated from the delicious grapes, I will still let it taste good to me. Tomorrow I will probably arrive in Bonn; it is raining unceasingly this afternoon, I have therefore overslept; the day after tomorrow to Cölln. Where you should address letters to me, I can hardly tell you anymore; I will not be able to receive an answer to this letter before 12 days, by then I will have long since passed Brussels; to Amsterdam via Emden, later Hamburg.... Greetings especially to Mr. Privy Councillor Schulze; — this evening I intend to visit Mr. Government Councillor Lange.

card: The previous day Hegel saw Romeo and Juliet performed by the English company in Paris, with Kemble as Romeo. In this staging Juliet wakes in the last act while Romeo, who has already taken the poison, is still alive. In the first-meeting scene Romeo sits beside Juliet before speaking, and Mercutio jokes with the Nurse when she interrupts them.
X:
My dear Marie,

Paris still holds me. Yesterday I saw the Englishman Shakespeare performed. Kemble as Romeo is dignified, but the play itself disappoints. They keep Juliet awake while Romeo is still alive – an unnecessary hesitation that dilutes the death. And then this custom: Romeo sits down next to Juliet before he speaks a word. It is a ridiculous confusion of physical proximity and ethical connection. Love is not mere contact, but a recognition of the spirit in the Other. Mercutio chatters with the Nurse while the lovers remain silent? That is comedy where tragedy is required. We Germans know the inner necessity better. I drink my wine, think of the order of our affairs at home, and am grateful that our sons in Berlin are learning the disciplined seriousness that is so often lacking here.

Your faithful Wilhelm
Y: Yesterday I saw Romeo and Juliet by the English troupe, — Juliet was very good, although not of the first rank, — not as much as Mde. Crelinger 2), — Romeo—Kemble was quite mediocre in the first four acts, without any life, — but in the last one, dreadful, mad, — I have now seen the English fury in its full glory; it is wonderful how they butcher Shakespeare; in the last act Juliet awakens while Romeo is still alive, but has already drunk the poison, — here is a scene in which she becomes completely out of her mind with madness and rages most horribly. — The scene of the first meeting of Romeo and Juliet is butchered in the same way, he already loves her beforehand, sits down next to her on the chair before he speaks to her, and when she is interrupted by the Nurse, Mercutio makes fun of her so that they can stay together and talk longer. —

card: When Hegel got off the express coach in Kassel the previous evening, a young man was already waiting for him on behalf of his father, Conrector Matthias, the father of one of Hegel's students, to invite him to stay at their house. Hegel declined.
X: This is my entire experience since you saw me depart. — Now a request — that you hand one of the copies of my Encyclopedia to Mr. Beer in my name, which I otherwise still reserve the right to inscribe; — I had forgotten to do so before my departure. When I alighted from the express post yesterday evening, a young man was already waiting for me, in the name of his father, the Vice-Principal Matthias, the father of one of my listeners, to invite me to stay with him, which I naturally did not accept. Paper is as far as the matter is exhausted. — In the afternoon or tomorrow morning I will probably set out with a hired carriage. Greet the young ones.
Y:
My dear Marie,

I arrive in Kassel in the evening and am tired from the journey. Last evening, upon arrival, a young man was already here, sent by Conrector Matthias, the father of one of my Berlin students. He earnestly invited me to stay with them. I declined.

It is a polite gesture that I do not wish to rudely reject, but I am not a guest who forces himself into other people's households, especially not on a journey that takes me through various territories. I prefer to stay in the city itself, to organize my thoughts and plan the next day. There is a certain dignity in remaining independent, even when one is received kindly.

I hope you and the children are well. The air here is fresher than in Berlin. I will write to you again soon.

Your faithful
G. W. F. Hegel

card: Hegel arrived in Luxembourg by diligence; Herr von Hanfstengel took him on a walk through the town and part of the fortifications. He booked the diligence to Metz for the next morning. A fellow passenger from Löwen, returning from a Rhine tour after losing a son of 21 and a daughter of 17, invited Hegel to visit him there.
X:
My dear Marie,

I arrived in Luxembourg this evening. Mr. von Hanfstengel showed me around the city and along the fortress walls; the fortifications are massive, but the air here is heavy. I have already secured the spot for the coach to Metz for tomorrow morning.

On the journey, a gentleman from Leuven sat next to me, who had just returned from a Rhine river cruise. He spoke with a quiet sorrow that deeply moved me: He has just lost a son of twenty-one and a daughter of seventeen years. The story reminds me that the individual is always subject to the universal, and how the freedom of the spirit in such moments collides with the harsh reality of death. He invited me to visit him in Leuven, which I gratefully declined, as my route to France compels me. I wish you and the boys all the best and kiss you.

Your
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: I have been here for an hour; I drove here in good company. I am here beyond the German border, but not yet within the French one; nor is even that exact, for this part of the Netherlands still belongs to the German Confederation. — I am returning tired from a walk that Mr. von Hanfstengel led me on, through the town and a part of the fortifications. The latter are admirable, so that I can see it too; — I have registered for the diligence to Metz and will depart there tomorrow morning, and from there it goes on to the real goal of the journey, to which the previous part was the preludes. You see that I am not exaggerating. The physical fatigues are not significant, the mental ones consist in the lack of business and the lack of conversation with you, in contrast to a conversation with insignificant company; yet this also goes quite well overall; a good Brabantine from Louvain, who had made a tour to the Rhine to distract himself from the recently suffered loss of a son of 21 years and a daughter of 17 years, was today with us in our diligence, a composed, restrained man, who invited me to visit him in Louvain.

card: On Sunday Hegel drank at the Töplitz spring, walked in the Clary park, bathed and went up the Schlackenberg again, then left by carriage at 11. He crossed a range of hills in about 1½ hours, with a view to Lowositz, then crossed the Eger twice, the second time by moonlight, towards Meldros. On Monday he reached Prague at 11.
X: On Sunday I still drank from the fountain, then went to the beautiful Clary Park, then took a bath, then went once more to the slag heap to finally take in the charming view, — then got into the carriage at 11 o'clock, — first over the second of the mountain ranges mentioned above, — everything fertile, rich, varied, — hills full of fields, meadow valleys, villages, fruit trees; after the mountain had been crossed in about 1 ½ hours, it goes from now on downhill or level (except for some small elevations) to Prague, — from the height of the mountain, into this other plane, an unbounded view to Lowositz, just as varied and rich, — from here flat country, boring fruit fields, — twice over the Eger — the second time with the most beautiful reflections of the moonlight towards Meldros. — Today through equally boring country, until the point where I suddenly looked down into the Moldau valley and onto Prague, — indeed a pleasant view shrouded in fragrance — and arrived there at 11 o'clock. — So I am writing this in Prague, and here there are immediately two interesting points: the one is Uncle, the other a letter from you, which needs to be seen and asked about
Y:
My dear Marie,

This afternoon I arrived in Prague. The journey from Töplitz was tiring, but the change of scene did me good. On Sunday I swam in the Töplitz spring and took a walk in the Clary Park. The air there is pure, and the quiet in the hills near Lowositz refreshed me greatly. I crossed the Eger river twice, the second time by moonlight, which had a strange, silent effect.

Now I am sitting in my room. The city is large and lively, but I miss our four walls in Berlin and the company of the children. Please forgive my absence; the journey was necessary to clear my mind before I think about the next lectures.

Give me news of Karl and Immanuel soon. Kiss me, if you can.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

card: Hegel was in Coblenz, writing at a window overlooking the Rhine, the bridge and Ehrenbreitstein, while eating grapes. He had been to the post office early that morning and found no letter from Marie. It was Immanuel's birthday, and he intended to drink an extra glass to him at midday.
X:
My dear Marie,

I am sitting in Koblenz at the window, which overlooks the Rhine and the Ehrenbreitstein Castle, and eating grapes, which are so sweet here that one could easily forget that one is far from home. Early in the morning I was at the post office, hopeful for a sign from you, but the drawer was empty. It is Immanuel's birthday, and I have resolved to drink an extra glass to his health at noon. It is a loss not to have him here to toast him personally, but his name tastes particularly good in the wine today.

The landscape is grand, but the silence is oppressive. I think of Karl and of you both. Please write to me soon, whether you are well. I will undertake the journey to Holland as soon as the post is secure.

Your faithful Wilhelm
Y: Here I sit, my dear, fulfilling my purpose, namely being in Coblenz, sitting by a window that overlooks the Rhine, my darling, the bridge, and Ehrenbreitstein, eating grapes, but what grapes! the sweetest, most delicious—and thinking of you all together and writing to you. I was at the post office this morning, but found no letter from you; in Cologne, however, I hope, if none more from you is addressed here and reaches me, then to find one. — On Immanuel’s birthday I shall drink an extra glass this noon, and as you will also be drinking to my well-being today, — so let it be hereby formally clinked! — But there is no fine weather today for fireworks; you, in any case, are taking proper care of yourself?). — I certainly do not yet know for sure one main thing, yet I can hardly doubt, namely that our dear mother should be among those celebrating and clinking; she will therefore also be included in the image of the table with which I am clinking. — So, general salvo, universal long live!

card: Hegel obtained his ticket for the express coach. The day before, he had been told that all seats for Tuesday and Friday were taken, though passengers could still apply for extra coaches. When he enquired that day, three people from Prague applied at the same time, but for Wednesday rather than Tuesday, so he took a seat for Wednesday.
X: Now all uncertainty has finally been put to an end, and I have the express coach ticket in my pocket. — Yesterday I received the answer that all seats for Tuesday and Friday were taken, but that persons might perhaps still be found for separate coaches. — Upon today’s inquiry, three Prague residents presented themselves along with me, but instead for Tuesday — for Wednesday; so I had to, against my will — but to be certain of the matter — concede one day. In 36 hours I shall then be in Prague and half the distance closer to you, — if only this second half could be covered just as quickly, to be soon with you, my dear, and among you, — there first to rest with you — to tell you — though little will remain that I have not already told in writing — to let you tell me all the more — and also to work.
Y:
My dear Marie,

I have finally secured a seat on the express coach for Wednesday. Yesterday I learned that Tuesday and Friday were already fully booked, but that extra carriages could be requested. So I inquired today, and since three travelers from Prague were simultaneously inquiring about Wednesday, I immediately secured a seat for myself.

It is a little comedy of chances how things are turning out. I am looking forward to the journey to Prague; the landscape is said to be magnificent. Please let me know how the boys are doing and whether you have received the post from Berlin. I often think of our house and the peace we enjoy there.

Allow yourself a glass of wine and think of me.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

card: In the morning Hegel visited the picture gallery and the art exhibition and went up onto the Brühl Terrace, where he had also been the day before. He had also spent an hour with Ammon. After finishing his letter he was going back to the gallery and then to Tieck.
X:
My dear Marie,

I am in Dresden this evening. The air here is heavy and warm, but I have recovered. Early tomorrow morning I was in the Picture Gallery and looked at the new exhibition. People speak a lot about Romanticism, but I stick to my judgment: Art must represent the True as a whole, not just moods or individual sensibilities. The works that pleased me were those in which the individual subordinated itself to the universal.

After that, I went to the Brühl Terrace. The view of the Elbe is magnificent, and one feels free there, as if standing above everyday worries. I conversed with Mr. Ammon for an hour. He is a witty man, and we spoke about the development of the spirit in art history. It is good to have such conversations, for the loneliness of travel becomes more bearable through exchange with other minds.

I am now going back to the Gallery to check a few more details, and then I will visit Tieck. He is here and will surely tell me a lot about the literary trends in Vienna.

Greetings to the boys. Kiss.

Your G. W. F. Hegel
Y: This morning the Gallery and art exhibition; onto the Brühl Terrace, where the view pleased me somewhat better today, yesterday it made little impression on me, — I have had quite enough of Dresden; — not to forget that I spent an hour at Ammon’s, — so today after this letter still to the Gallery and to Tiek. Now I hope in Prague to receive a letter from

card: Hegel spent the whole day on his feet in the Esterhazy gallery and at Schönbrunn, where he ate, and was due at the Italian opera half an hour after writing. The weather had cleared the previous afternoon, and the day was fine and not too hot.
X: I am adding another sheet and scribbling a bit more, although I am dull and tired — from standing and walking all day in the Esterházy Gallery and in Schönbrunn, where I ate; since the Italian opera is about to begin in half an hour, I will not engage in any further reports, only that it cleared up yesterday afternoon, and today the weather is the most beautiful in the world, not too hot and promising consistency. — Flesh and blood have struggled with the will — to hasten to meet you from here on Friday, October 1st; however, you give me permission to stay longer, I have seen and enjoyed everything in the whirlwind; I have been diligent, on my feet all day, and there is still much to see; — in order to preserve the good and create for myself a treasure of memory, I must see it once more, — of course I will not see the Italian opera for a second time; the beautiful, infinitely varied, lovely countryside I have only just experienced today, and savored in what beautiful sunshine.
Y:
My dear Marie,

It was a magnificent day. After yesterday's rain, the air was clear, and the heat was bearable. I spent the hours in the Esterházy Gallery and subsequently in the Schönbrunn Palace Park, where I had lunch. The walks did me good; one must keep moving if one wishes to keep the mind fresh.

Soon I shall make my way to the Italian Opera House. I hope the music will refresh me, which is necessary after so much walking. Think of me when you think of the cool evening air in Vienna. The children will probably be envious of my career as an adventurer.

Take care of yourself.

Your G. W. F. Hegel

card: Hegel left Prague after 11 o'clock and travelled in sunshine through the Bohemian countryside and its villages. By evening there was a full moon. He expected to reach Töplitz at noon the next day and Dresden the following evening, or perhaps only on Sunday.
X:
Prague, October 8.

My dear Marie,

I left the city this afternoon and traveled through bright, sunlit Bohemia. The villages lay in the light, and as night fell, the full moon stood in the sky – a sight that reminded me of our shared hours in Berlin. I have resolved to be in Töplitz by noon tomorrow to enjoy the baths there. From there, I will continue my journey to Dresden; perhaps I will not reach the city on the Elbe until Sunday.

The air is fresh, and I feel lively. Please give my regards to the boys and tell Ludwig that I will soon be back in Berlin to tell him the stories of my journey. I often think of you and our quiet evenings.

Your faithful
G. W. F. Hegel
Y: From Prague I traveled through Bohemia, which is so beautiful in its views—though the Bohemian villages are wretched and no longer seem Bohemian to me now—in the most beautiful, loveliest sunshine, which beautifies everything, just as the full moonlight and a few thin candles now gild my memory of you. Tomorrow at noon I will arrive in Töplitz, and tomorrow evening, perhaps not until Sunday, in Dresden.

card: Hegel walked in the park along the Ilm. At 2 p.m. he dined at Goethe's, seated beside him, with Fräulein von Pogwisch, Hofrat Vogel, Dr. Emmerich (Goethe's secretary), the two grandsons, Goethe's son and Zelter; Frau von Goethe, expecting her confinement, was absent. Hegel told Goethe about politics and literature in France. That evening he went to the theatre.
X: I had to take possession of the [illegible/abbreviated term], in order to encounter it. — Then a walk along the old, familiar paths of the beautiful park, trodden 25 years ago, greeting the banks of the little Ilm and its quieter waves, which have heard many an immortal song. At 2 o’clock to lunch at Goethe’s, which was excellent and honored by the best appetite; — Mrs. von Goethe!) is, expecting her delivery every hour, invisible, — so she was not at the table, — the sister, Miss von Pogwisch), quite lively, Court Councillor Vogel the doctor, a Mr. Emmerich), Goethe’s secretary, the two grandchildren, the son, Zelter and I — I sat next to Goethe, on my right the aforementioned Miss; the Weimar guests quieter, but we cheerful, conversational, eating and drinking bravely, — I had to tell Goethe a great deal about the political and literary views and interests in France, he was very interested in everything; he is quite strong, healthy, generally the old, i.e. always young — somewhat quieter — such a venerable, good, faithful head, that one forgets the great man of genius and inexhaustible energy of talent; we are as old, faithful friends anyway not on the footing of observation, — how he appears or what he has spoken, but cordially together, and not for the sake of boasting and honor, that of having seen and heard him, etc. — The son told me very explicitly after the meal how Goethe had rejoiced in the hope that I would call on him on my return journey from Paris; he spoke to me in general in detail about his relationship and feelings towards his father in every respect, and one must praise Goethe in his age and way of life as happy, knowing him in such love and care, and respect and love the son for it. This evening I was then also at the theater, — and now I am writing this to you, — and what I have principally to add is about our plans or rather decisions, finally to go home. Goethe would therefore have Zelter and me with him at least tomorrow; so we travel the day after tomorrow; Zelter just as satisfied that I am with him, as I am that he makes the further journey with me. But since we are both old gentlemen by now and convenience is agreeable and useful to us, we are not inclined to the bravery of the express post,... but we will depart on Friday with the hired coach, which we have already hired, and, if God wills, arrive at your place on Sunday, where your Odysseus, after the multicolored voyages, will return to the monochromaticity of domestic life (returning!) to embrace you.
Y:
My dear Marie,

Weimar receives me with a warmth that makes me long for Berlin, where you await me. The air here is mild, but my heart remains with our sons.

Lunch at Goethe’s was an event. I sat next to him; his wit is still sharp despite his age. Mrs. von Goethe was absent, which somewhat clouded the mood, yet the company was lively. I spoke with him about the state of affairs in France, both in politics and literature. He listened to me, as he does, with that quiet, superior attention. It is interesting how he views things from his own perspective, beyond academic debates.

In the evening I went to the theater. The play was decent, but nothing remarkable. I am tired, but content. Please give my regards to Karl and Immanuel, and tell Ludwig that I am thinking of him.

Your faithful
G. Hegel

card: The previous day Hegel visited Versailles and the Grand and Petit Trianon. The Trianons are furnished; the palace is not. The garden has 130 marble statues, and the oldest tree in the orangery was planted in 1420. The Trianon grounds are in the English style, with artificial rocks and Swiss cottages. He did not see the fountains play.
X:
My dear Marie,

Paris, in the evening. Yesterday I visited Versailles. The main building is still empty, which gives off a certain desolation, but the Trianons are furnished. They have laid out the garden there in so-called English style: artificial rocks, Swiss huts – a kind of arbitrary arrangement that seeks to outdo the natural order. In the orangery stands a tree that was planted in 1420; its age is a silent admonition, while the 130 marble statues in the park remain merely stones.

It is strange how here history and the present touch each other without connecting. I saw no fountains, which troubled me little; water is not necessary to recognize the essence of things, even though it sharpens the sense of the eternal. My heart is with you in Berlin. The journey is arduous, but the thoughts are sharp.

Your faithful Wilhelm
Y: Yesterday I was in Versailles and saw the splendors there, including the Grand and Petit Trianon. The latter two are furnished, but the Palace of Versailles is not, so one sees only the splendor of its doors, walls, ceilings, and wall paintings. The latter are mostly entirely new and mediocre. The gardens are too old-fashioned French: wide squares with clipped hedges, groves, separate side plantings of trees, fountains, statues, colonnades, and so on. The number of marble statues in the garden is 130. The orangery is admirable, and the oldest tree was planted in the year 1420. In contrast, the Trianons have English, charming layouts, though also with whimsical artificial rocks and Swiss-style cottages. The greatest fuss is made about the jumping of the water, which we did not see, only the multitude of Neptunes, Tritons, frogs, and so on.

card: Hegel passed through Herzberg at midday on Monday, where a country preacher's niece joined him as far as Dresden. On arrival he found Privy Councillor Schulze at his inn and persuaded him to delay his departure by a day. That morning the two visited Böttiger, the picture gallery and Böttiger's lecture, where they went through the antiquities again.
X:
My dear Marie,

I am sitting in the inn in Dresden and writing to you as night falls. The journey here was lively. At Herzberg at midday, I was accompanied by the niece of a country parson, who accompanied me all the way here.

Upon arriving here, I found the Privy Councillor Schulze, whom I persuaded to postpone his departure by one day. We spent the day together: A visit to Böttiger, the painting collection, and his lecture. We went through the antiquities together once more; it is good to share such things with a friend who shares the same interest.

I think of you and the boys. Berlin is far, but my thoughts are with you. The air here is pleasant, and I am taking the time I need on the journey.

Stay healthy.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel
Y: The journey has been ordinary and, despite the change in weather, very bearable; on Sunday the sky was overcast — it rained a few times — until Jüterbog; then on Monday, after midday, I arrived in Herzberg, where I had a country parson invite his niece to keep me company until Dresden; she was not ugly, already well into her years, so insignificant and Saxonly polite that I had little more desire or occasion to speak than if I had been traveling alone; so I think nothing ill of this company; had I, however, become a proper Englishman on my travels, I would not have let myself be talked out of it, but would have kept to myself; but as one is still a bit of a German, I could not refuse, and besides — as we Swabians say — I bought the cat in the sack, and the result was not uneven, but insignificant. — Upon arrival I went straight to the inn, where I heard that Privy Councillor Schulze was lodging (— I naturally took rooms at the Blue Star) — I luckily met him and, after he had already arranged everything for his departure today, persuaded him to stay with me until this evening; we were both greatly pleased to meet.... This morning I went with Schulze first to Böttiger, then to the picture gallery, then to Böttiger’s lecture, where we went through the antiquities again.

card: Hegel travelled from Amsterdam via Utrecht and Deventer, then by post wagon with a gentleman from Hildesheim, Mr. Cludius, reaching Osnabrück at 5 am on Wednesday; there he visited Prof. Abeken and saw the hall of the Peace of Westphalia. He reached Bremen Thursday at nightfall and Hamburg by express post on 18 October, seeing fireworks there that evening.
X:
My dear Marie,

I have reached Hamburg. The journey through the Netherlands was arduous, but the way from Deventer to Osnabrück with Mr. Cludius passed in pleasant conversation. There I visited Professor Abeken and saw the Hall of the Peace of Westphalia; a place of great historical significance, which carries the spirit of the times within it.

This evening I experienced a fireworks display in Hamburg. It was a luminous spectacle that illuminated the night – a fitting conclusion to a long day. I hope Karl and Immanuel are well. Please give my regards to Ludwig.

I enjoy the change, but my heart is in Berlin, with you. I will return soon to continue my lectures.

Yours
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: ...badly balanced), my journey up to now had gone quite happily, though it was marred by the lack of news from you; but now, after I received news of you in Amsterdam, the trouble has struck the journey. So instead of taking the direct route here, the waiters—everything went too fast for me to be able to inquire more precisely—put me on the diligence to Utrecht, where I spent the night. From here it went at half past nine in the morning to Deventer. From Utrecht, which is likewise a beautiful city with a university and charming surroundings—farewell beautiful Holland and Brabant—from here it is all heath, though still covered with shrubbery. In Deventer I spent the night again and got on a genuine German post coach.... It was dear to me not to have been sitting on this coach from the point of its departure, otherwise I would not have been able to spend the previous night in a bed either. — So it went day and night—through desolate heaths, though interrupted by some oases—Bentheim lies on a rocky hill, charming with a magnificent unbounded view over the fertile little country—on; we drank good coffee in Dutch kitchens—if I were to have a house built, I would have such a kitchen installed too—but there was no time for a proper lunch;—it crept slowly along in the sand, or on the better paved road it was even worse. — In this torture chamber we stayed until Wednesday morning at 5 o'clock, when we arrived in Osnabrück?). I gratefully remember my traveling companion, a gentleman from Hildesheim—Mr. Cludius, if I am right—with whom I was quite calm and trusting, in contrast to the previous silent Dutch model chart-makers, who could not speak with me and were equally unwilling to make much conversation among themselves. In Osnabrück I slept a few hours very soundly and then sought out a former Jena auditor, Prof. Abeken), a brother of the Berlin one whom you often met at Partheys', whom I was truly glad to see again, and who accompanied me in the most friendly manner. The surroundings of Osnabrück are quite charming; I also saw the hall where the Peace of Westphalia was concluded;—at about 3 o'clock I got on the diligence going to Bremen, and in Diepholz I parted from my good Hildesheim gentleman, who was going to Hanover. The road was in very beautiful sunshine, which I pitied for having to shine on such steppes—though towards Bremen Dutch green meadows—with the night we arrived there yesterday (Thursday), slept until this morning, from where I transferred myself here by extra post. The heavens rained on the Bremen citizens' October 18th Patriotism this morning; but the evening allowed me to clearly see the Hamburg rockets and other fireworks...

card: Two days earlier, after a first night in a supplementary coach with four passengers, Hegel reached Halle at midday, fetched Hinrichs, ate and slept in the afternoon; at 6 p.m. he left for Nordhausen with one student and slept most of the night. The previous day, from 6 a.m., he travelled with students from Nordhausen to Kassel.
X:
Kassel, August 19

My dear Marie,

I am writing to you from the inn. The journey through Hesse was long and tiring. After the first night's ride in the overstuffed post coach, we reached Halle at noon. There I picked up Hinrichs, and we ate and slept in the afternoon. At six o'clock we continued on to Nordhausen, where I spent the night with a student. Early yesterday morning, at six, we resumed the journey with students to Kassel.

My head is full of roads, dust, and the murmuring of travelers. The landscape here is hilly, but nothing that would keep my thoughts away from you. I am tired, but my spirit is awake.

Give my kisses to Karl and Immanuel. Tell Ludwig that I am thinking of him. I hope the wine in Berlin is good and that the cards went well in the evenings.

Your faithful
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: The journey itself so far has certainly not been without discomfort; the first night was the worst, it was far too cramped in the cabriolet, — I moved into the side-chaise, where, however, we were four, and at every station we got a different and always a worse one. From Wittenberg it went better. — At noon we arrived in Halle, the company had diminished; I fetched Hinrichs, ate lunch, slept very well in the afternoon, — at 6 we departed for Nordhausen, only one student with me — an excellent express coach — each person took a side, the bench was like a sofa, I settled myself on it and, as you know, I am accustomed to sleeping on the sofa, slept almost the whole night. — Yesterday and the day before yesterday the most beautiful weather, — but in the first night it rained very heavily from midnight on; — always in the company of students we made the journey from Nordhausen to here yesterday from 6 in the morning.

card: Hegel was lodging in Brussels with Mr. van Ghert, at whose house he had spent the night. On arriving the previous evening he had gone straight to the letter post, but the office was already closed. His only news from Marie so far was the letter he received in Cassel; he would learn within the hour whether more had come.
X:
My dear Marie,

I am here in Brussels, with the kind Mr. van Ghert, who has received me with the greatest friendliness. The city is large, but the streets still confuse me. Last evening, as I hurried to the post office to look for news from you, the office was already closed – a small inconvenience that spoiled my evening.

My only news from you is still the letter from Kassel, which I brought with me. I am now waiting impatiently for the postman; within an hour I hope to learn whether any further letters have arrived. Until then, I sit here, drink a glass of wine, and try to endure the heat.

Think of me, my wife, and forgive me that I have so little time to write to you in more detail. I will answer immediately tomorrow morning, as soon as I know whether everything is in order.

Your faithful G. W. F. Hegel
Y: So you see now, my dear, that I am at the end of my journey, that is, approximately at the most distant point of it, — approximately, for there will probably still be a small excursion into the neighborhood, but my main direction will now be home, towards you; but until now I have had no news from you beyond the letter I received in Cassel; last evening I went straight to the post office after my arrival, but the office was already closed; now it will be seen in an hour whether there are letters from you there q.... In the meantime I will only tell you that I am lodged here with Mr. van Ghert, who did nothing else, and spent the night with him and am feeling quite well. — I wrote to you from Cölln. On Sunday morning I had Wallraf’s paintings shown to me now in daylight; among them was the main picture, the Death of Mary, undoubtedly by the same Master Schoreel, from whom the picture of the same subject, which belongs to Boisseree, and which you have also always loved so much, is; — the Wallraf one is smaller, about 2¼ feet high, but wider. The donor on one wing, like the woman on the other, are exactly the same portraits, they were complete old acquaintances to me — the arrangement of the figures in the picture, the position of the bed etc. is different. — After I had attended the service in the cathedral in Cölln and taken my leave of the good people who had received me so friendly, I drove to Aachen in the afternoon, — in good company with an elderly Englishman who had become a German and a lawyer from Cölln, who always carries Goethe’s Faust as his Bible on his person, while at the same time being quite pleased with himself in an unreserved way. We arrived at 10 o’clock at night. In Aachen I saw the cathedral first, sat on Emperor Charles’s chair; there are two marble plates on the sides, also on the backrest, smooth, 1⅛ inch thick;

card: Hegel and Mr. van Ghert walked the Waterloo battlefield for 3–4 hours on Friday and on Saturday saw the Brussels gallery, St. Gudula church and Laeken palace. On Sunday afternoon they went to Ghent, attended the university's rectorate handover there on Monday until 1 o'clock, then left by cabriolet at 2:30, reaching the Scheldt bank opposite Antwerp after 10 pm.
X: It has been a few days since I have had the first quiet hour in which I am alone and can continue the account of my journey to you, my dear. On Friday we visited the battlefield of Waterloo in a carriage, and I saw here these eternally memorable fields, hills, and points—especially the high, wooded hill stood out to me, from which one can see many miles in every direction, where Napoleon, the prince of battles, had set up his throne, which he lost here! In the stifling midday heat we walked for three to four hours on the paths, where under every clod of earth brave men lie buried. On Saturday we saw the picture gallery, strolled in the park, visited St. Gudula’s Church, and examined its beautiful windows—the most beautiful I have ever seen—its paintings, marble statues, and so on. Then in the evening we went to Laeken Palace—a pleasant walk and a nice spot. On Sunday morning was spent with going out, visiting churches, shopping for you, my dear, and packing, and at half past two o’clock we drove together—Mr. van Ghert had the kindness, and coincidentally also, as a convalescent from an illness, the leisure to accompany me—to Ghent. Here we saw the beautiful cathedral, some other churches, and then attended the act of the handover of the rectorship of the university, which lasted until one o’clock, then quickly ate lunch, and at half past three o’clock drove here in a carriage, where we arrived yesterday after ten o’clock, just opposite from here, on the other bank of the Scheldt.
Y:
Antwerp, 8 October 1822

My dearest Marie,

The journey has been vigorous. Van Ghert and I walked the fields of Waterloo for three hours, a landscape still heavy with the memory of that decisive blow to the old order. We then viewed the galleries in Brussels and the church of St. Gudula, before proceeding to Ghent. The academic handover there was tedious, but I endured it with the necessary dignity.

We departed Ghent by cabriolet at half past two, arriving here only after ten o’clock, exhausted by the long ride along the Scheldt. The city is bustling, the commercial spirit palpable. I am weary but content. Do not worry for me; I shall rest well and hope to continue northward soon.

Give my love to the boys. I think of you and our home in Berlin often.

Yours ever,
G. W. F. Hegel

card: Hegel and his companion had spent a night at Flamandsch Hooft (Point of Flanders). Their road was paved like the Königsstraße in Berlin, tree-lined, and ran between fields, gardens and meadows; unlike around Aachen and Liège they met no beggars, village children wore shoes, many of them wooden, and stockings, and they passed through a village of 15,000 inhabitants.
X:
My dear Marie,

We spent the night in Flamen Hoofd. The road here is paved like the Kings Road in Berlin, lined with trees, and stretches between fields, gardens, and meadows. In contrast to Aachen and Liège, we saw not a single beggar here. The village children wear shoes, many of them wooden, and stockings. We drove through a village of 15,000 inhabitants. It is a pleasant change from what we were accustomed to in the eastern provinces. The order here is visible and calm. I am drinking a good wine and writing you these few lines to tell you about our journey. Karl and Immanuel will surely be curious, but I hope they will learn more from this order than from mere storytelling. The freedom that I recognize in the German spirit manifests itself here in the quiet of everyday life, not in the noise. I think of you in Berlin, where life has its own rhythm. Until soon, I kiss you.

Your G.W.F. Hegel
Y: Michelangelo made it, to see — by Michelangelo! Where else in Germany can one see a work by this master? — But to continue the report, we stayed overnight in Flamandsch Hooft (Tip of Flanders). — It is, as said, a pleasure to travel in this country; all the country roads are paved like the Königsstraße in Berlin, alongside the road are all fruit fields, gardens or meadows, and the highway is planted with trees. — From Aachen to Liège it swarms with beggars, up to here we have not met a single one; one sees adults and children in the villages only well-dressed and playing happily, no child in rags, none without shoes (many wooden shoes) and stockings, — we passed through a village of 15,000 inhabitants. —

card: At 10 o'clock the previous evening, while Hegel was waiting for soup in his room in Kassel, Heinrich Beer and his wife walked in; the meeting was unplanned. Beer was returning directly from Kassel and could tell Marie that he had found Hegel well.
X:
Kassel, August 19.

My dear Marie,

I experienced a most pleasant surprise this evening. While I was waiting for my soup at the inn, Heinrich Beer and his wife suddenly entered my room. It was a completely unplanned meeting, as Beer was just returning from here and happened to pass by.

He was kind enough to tell me that he found me in the best of health. For me, it was a reassuring sight to see an acquaintance who knows me and whose opinion of my condition I value. I hope he did not tell you anything about the heat or my travel discomforts, which I anyway consider mere imagination.

I am still well and enjoy the quiet that is offered here. The evenings are pleasant. I hope Karl and Immanuel are in good health and are diligently occupied with their studies, as befits young men who are working on their minds.

Kiss the children.

Your G. W. F. Hegel
Y: Good morning, my dear! I was just thinking last evening, while I was waiting for my bowl of soup, whether I should start writing to you yet — it was 10 o’clock — as whom? — Mr. Heinrich Beer!) — and his wife — entered my room. You can imagine the joy we felt at this so unexpected meeting; since he is going directly back from here, he can tell you that he found me in good health.
